items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>enter</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to enter</vocabulary> word are the same character with the same meaning. This is the intransitive one: you walk in under your own steam, nobody pushes you through the door.
items.reading_mnemonic: Leaning forward, one leg stepping ahead, you duck under the low doorway calling <reading>hi, Ruth</reading>, and on <reading>はいる</reading> you <vocabulary form="入る">enter</vocabulary> under your own steam.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は部屋に入ります。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は部屋[へや]に入[はい]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は店に入った。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は店[みせ]に入[はい]った。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が家に入る。
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が家[いえ]に入[はい]る。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>exit</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to leave / go out</vocabulary> word are the same character with the same meaning. This is the intransitive one: you head out yourself, you are not shoved out by anyone.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>deer</reading> trapped in the lidless box stacks loose rocks into a little mountain and climbs out over the top, <reading>でる</reading>, to <vocabulary form="出る">leave</vocabulary> on its own hooves.

example_sentences.japanese: 朝、家を出ます。
example_sentences.english: I leave the house in the morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]、家[いえ]を出[で]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は駅を出た。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は駅[えき]を出[で]た。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が部屋から出た。
example_sentences.english: The cat came out of the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が部屋[へや]から出[で]た。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A badger in a peaked cap hauls itself up into the night bus and grabs the rail as the bus pulls away. That scramble up onto a moving vehicle is what it means to <vocabulary>board</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The badger's electric bus rolls up with <reading>no roar</reading> at all, so you almost miss it in the dark. Jump on before the doors close and you 「<reading>のる</reading>」 — you <vocabulary>ride</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はバスに乗ります。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はバスに乗[の]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅でタクシーに乗りました。
example_sentences.english: I took a taxi at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]でタクシーに乗[の]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: どこでバスに乗りますか。
example_sentences.english: Where do you get on the bus?
example_sentences.furigana: どこでバスに乗[の]りますか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The chairlift on the mountain trail carries you up, and where the cable turns you <kanji>descend</kanji> from the seat onto the snow. That hop down off the lift is how you <vocabulary>get off</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ori the lift attendant sighs <reading>'oh, really'</reading> at every skier who freezes on the unloading ramp. Only when they hear his flat 「<reading>おりる</reading>」 do they finally <vocabulary>get off</vocabulary> the chair.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は駅で降ります。
example_sentences.english: I get off at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は駅[えき]で降[お]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: バスを降りました。
example_sentences.furigana: バスを降[お]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: どこで降りますか。
example_sentences.furigana: どこで降[お]りますか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>ford</kanji> the shallow river stepping stone by stepping stone until you reach the far bank. Getting all the way to the other side is what it means to <vocabulary>cross</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Each step the heron takes through the <reading>water</reading> makes a slow suck and slap, 「<reading>わたる</reading>」, as it works toward the other side. That patient wade is the bird choosing to <vocabulary>cross</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 道を渡ります。
example_sentences.furigana: 道[みち]を渡[わた]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: あの橋を渡りました。
example_sentences.furigana: あの橋[はし]を渡[わた]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 子供が川を渡る。
example_sentences.furigana: 子[こ]供[ども]が川[かわ]を渡[わた]る。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The straight road suddenly hits a <kanji>bend</kanji> and swings hard to the left. Following that bend around is what it means to <vocabulary>turn</vocabulary> a corner.
items.reading_mnemonic: Your driving <reading>guru</reading> sits silent on the straight road until it swings hard left at the bend, then barks <reading>まがる</reading> and you follow it round to <vocabulary form="曲がる">turn</vocabulary> the corner.

example_sentences.japanese: この角を曲がります。
example_sentences.furigana: この角[かど]を曲[ま]がります。

example_sentences.japanese: 角を曲がると駅がある。
example_sentences.english: When you turn the corner, there's a station.
example_sentences.furigana: 角[かど]を曲[ま]がると駅[えき]がある。

example_sentences.japanese: タクシーが角を曲がった。
example_sentences.furigana: タクシーが角[かど]を曲[ま]がった。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>stop</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>to stop</vocabulary> are the same character, so the meaning carries over. The trailing kana marks the intransitive one: something halts on its own, with nobody stopping it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle plants one foot flat, heel and toes dug in, and his <reading>tomato</reading> basket sways, <reading>とまる</reading>, as he comes to a <vocabulary form="止まる">stop</vocabulary> on his own.

example_sentences.japanese: バスが止まる。
example_sentences.furigana: バスが止[と]まる。

example_sentences.japanese: 雨が止まった。
example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]が止[と]まった。

example_sentences.japanese: ここで止まらないで。
example_sentences.furigana: ここで止[と]まらないで。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A race that the gun sends tearing off the line with nobody there to start it has simply come <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary> all by itself.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the school sports field the gun cracks and the kangaroo the kids call Jim is already gone. Shout <reading>Ha, Jim, a roo</reading> and you have <reading>はじまる</reading>, a race that came <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary> on its own.

example_sentences.japanese: 学校が八時に始まります。
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がっ]校[こう]が八[はち]時[じ]に始[はじ]まります。

example_sentences.japanese: 映画が今始まります。
example_sentences.furigana: 映[えい]画[が]が今[いま]始[はじ]まります。

example_sentences.japanese: 雨が始まりました。
example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]が始[はじ]まりました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You open the book, set the pace, and drive the class forward yourself, and making something start by your own hand like that is <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met this sound in 始まる, so the one where you start something yourself is <reading>はじめる</reading>, <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は本を読み始めます。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は本[ほん]を読[よ]み始[はじ]めます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日から勉強を始めます。
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]から勉[べん]強[きょう]を始[はじ]めます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は映画を見始めた。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は映[えい]画[が]を見[み]始[はじ]めた。

items.mnemonic_text: It comes to an end: owaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Follow a road all the way to its <kanji>end</kanji> and there is no more road left to walk. Something that runs itself out like that, with nobody stopping it, is <vocabulary>to finish</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You follow the road to where it runs out and find a walrus sprawled on the last stone; <reading>oh, walrus</reading>, you sigh, <reading>おわる</reading>, there is no more road and the walk can only <vocabulary form="終わる">finish</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 学校は三時に終わる。
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がっ]校[こう]は三[さん]時[じ]に終[お]わる。

example_sentences.japanese: 映画が終わった。
example_sentences.furigana: 映[えい]画[が]が終[お]わった。

example_sentences.japanese: 終わったら家に帰る。
example_sentences.english: When it finishes, I'll go home.
example_sentences.furigana: 終[お]わったら家[いえ]に帰[かえ]る。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You jab in the number and cackle your hello far too loudly down the line. That <reading>cackle-rue</reading> of a greeting is <reading>かける</reading>, which is <vocabulary>to make a call</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は母に電話をかけます。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は母[はは]に電[でん]話[わ]をかけます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日友達に電話をかけた。
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]友[とも]達[だち]に電[でん]話[わ]をかけた。

example_sentences.japanese: 誰に電話をかけますか。
example_sentences.furigana: 誰[だれ]に電[でん]話[わ]をかけますか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>cut</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to cut</vocabulary> word are the very same thing, so the る on the end just makes it the verb you do to something.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit takes a sword to one carrot seven times, then <reading>keel</reading>s over giggling at the bits on the board, <reading>きる</reading>: that is what it means to <vocabulary form="切る">cut</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 母が野菜を切ります。
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]が野[や]菜[さい]を切[き]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: この紙を切ってください。
example_sentences.furigana: この紙[かみ]を切[き]ってください。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟はパンを切った。
example_sentences.english: My little brother cut the bread.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]はパンを切[き]った。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You drag a jumper down over your head and force both arms through the sleeves until your face pops out the top. Winning that wrestling match with a shirt is what it means to <vocabulary>wear (top)</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A heron on the mountain trail is so cold it feeds coins to the vending machine and drags on a whole <reading>kilo</reading> of knitted jumpers. It squawks 「<reading>きる</reading>」 and will <vocabulary>wear (top)</vocabulary> anything with sleeves.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はシャツを着ます。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はシャツを着[き]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は新しい服を着た。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は新[あたら]しい服[ふく]を着[き]た。

example_sentences.japanese: 冬はコートを着ます。
example_sentences.english: In winter I wear a coat.
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]はコートを着[き]ます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The only way to <kanji>escape</kanji> a soaked raincoat is to peel it down off your arms and let it drop. Peeling a garment off your body like that is what it means to <vocabulary>take off (clothes)</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A walrus flops onto the riverbank and drags its dripping wetsuit off over its head. It grunts 「<reading>ぬぐ</reading>」 as a cold <reading>nugget</reading> of riverweed plops from the sleeve, because it will <vocabulary>take off (clothes)</vocabulary> anywhere.

example_sentences.japanese: 家で靴を脱ぎます。
example_sentences.english: I take off my shoes at home.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[いえ]で靴[くつ]を脱[ぬ]ぎます。

example_sentences.japanese: コートを脱いでください。
example_sentences.furigana: コートを脱[ぬ]いでください。

example_sentences.japanese: 暑いからシャツを脱ぐ。
example_sentences.english: I take off my shirt because it's hot.
example_sentences.furigana: 暑[あつ]いからシャツを脱[ぬ]ぐ。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You hold a filthy boot under the tap and work every seam with your thumbs until the water finally runs clear. Driving grime off a thing with water is what it means to <vocabulary>wash</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei's team tracks the whole muddy field into the hallway and kicks up <reading>a row</reading> over whose boots stink worst. Sei lines every boot at the tap, because someone has to <vocabulary>wash</vocabulary> the lot, and mutters 「<reading>あらう</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝手を洗います。
example_sentences.english: I wash my hands every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]手[て]を洗[あら]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は毎日髪を洗う。
example_sentences.english: My younger sister washes her hair every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は毎[まい]日[にち]髪[かみ]を洗[あら]う。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は服を洗いました。
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は服[ふく]を洗[あら]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Turn a knot of kids loose in a park and they run in looping circles for no reason and to no end. That aimless motion, done for its own sake, is what it means to <vocabulary>play</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Toss <reading>a soap</reading> bubble into the park and the knot of kids runs looping circles after it, for no reason and to no end, <reading>あそぶ</reading>: that is to <vocabulary form="遊ぶ">play</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で友達と遊ぶ。
example_sentences.english: I play with friends at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で友[とも]達[だち]と遊[あそ]ぶ。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日うちで遊んだ。
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]うちで遊[あそ]んだ。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末に海で遊ぶ。
example_sentences.english: I play at the sea on the weekend.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]に海[うみ]で遊[あそ]ぶ。

items.word_type: godan verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>song</kanji> sits silent on the page until a voice lifts it into the air. Pushing it out of your mouth like that is what it means to <vocabulary>sing</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The song lies silent on the page until you lift it into the air, ending on a proud <reading>you-ta-daa</reading>, <reading>うたう</reading>, and that push of voice is to <vocabulary form="歌う">sing</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は上手に歌う。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は上手[じょうず]に歌[うた]う。

example_sentences.japanese: 夜、友達と一緒に歌う。
example_sentences.english: At night I sing with my friends.
example_sentences.furigana: 夜[よる]、友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に歌[うた]う。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は歌うのが好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は歌[うた]うのが好[す]きです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Your hips swing, your feet cross and stamp, and your arms cut shapes in the air in time with a beat. All that patterned motion to music is what it means to <vocabulary>dance</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Your hips swing and your feet stamp in time with the beat until you crash into the <reading>odd door</reading> in the hall, <reading>おどる</reading>, still moving: that is to <vocabulary form="踊る">dance</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 週末に友達と踊ります。
example_sentences.english: I dance with friends on the weekend.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]に友[とも]達[だち]と踊[おど]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で一緒に踊りましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let's dance together in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で一[いっ]緒[しょ]に踊[おど]りましょう。

example_sentences.japanese: 子供が庭で踊っています。
example_sentences.english: The kids are dancing in the yard.
example_sentences.furigana: 子[こ]供[ども]が庭[にわ]で踊[おど]っています。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Your mouth pulls wide, your cheeks bunch up under your eyes, and air comes out of you in short barks you cannot hold back. That whole helpless reaction is what it means to <vocabulary>laugh / smile</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Your mouth pulls wide and the air bursts out in short barks, like a <reading>walrus</reading> you cannot hold back, <reading>わらう</reading>, which is what it is to <vocabulary form="笑う">laugh</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 友達が笑う。
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]が笑[わら]う。

example_sentences.japanese: 面白い映画を見て笑う。
example_sentences.english: I laugh watching a funny movie.
example_sentences.furigana: 面[おも]白[しろ]い映[えい]画[が]を見[み]て笑[わら]う。

example_sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんが今笑っている。
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]ちゃんが今[いま]笑[わら]っている。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Water wells up along your lower lids until it spills over and runs down in two warm lines, and your breath keeps catching in hiccups. All of that at once is what it means to <vocabulary>cry</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Each hiccup in your breath is a little <reading>knock</reading> in your chest while two warm lines run down your cheeks, <reading>なく</reading>, and that is what it is to <vocabulary form="泣く">cry</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんが今泣いています。
example_sentences.english: The baby is crying right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]ちゃんが今[いま]泣[な]いています。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は部屋で泣きました。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother cried in his room.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は部屋[へや]で泣[な]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 母の手紙を読んで泣いた。
example_sentences.english: I cried reading my mother's letter.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]の手[て]紙[がみ]を読[よ]んで泣[な]いた。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Everything that was keeping you going, heartbeat, breath, the warmth in your hands, switches off one part at a time and does not come back. That final shutdown is what it means to <vocabulary>die</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 祖父が去年死にました。
example_sentences.furigana: 祖[そ]父[ふ]が去[きょ]年[ねん]死[し]にました。

example_sentences.japanese: この木は冬に死ぬ。
example_sentences.furigana: この木[き]は冬[ふゆ]に死[し]ぬ。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬が死んで悲しい。
example_sentences.english: I'm sad that the dog died.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]が死[し]んで悲[かな]しい。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A brand-new <kanji>life</kanji> that was nowhere a minute ago and is suddenly here, breathing on its own. That sudden arrival is what it means to <vocabulary>be born</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>mare</reading> nickers as a foal that was nowhere a minute ago is suddenly here in the straw, breathing on its own, <reading>うまれる</reading>; that arrival is to <vocabulary form="生まれる">be born</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 来月赤ちゃんが生まれる。
example_sentences.english: A baby will be born next month.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]月[げつ]赤[あか]ちゃんが生[う]まれる。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は去年生まれました。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother was born last year.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は去[きょ]年[ねん]生[う]まれました。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫に子供が生まれた。
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]に子[こ]供[ども]が生[う]まれた。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>dwell</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>to live</vocabulary> are the same character carrying the same sense, so the meaning crosses straight over.
items.reading_mnemonic: A retired <reading>sumo</reading> wrestler is far too heavy to shift house, so for forty years he has done nothing but <vocabulary>reside</vocabulary> in one hut beside the shrine. A wrestler who never moves is one who only <reading>すむ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はここに住んでいます。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はここに住[す]んでいます。

example_sentences.japanese: どこに住んでいますか。
example_sentences.furigana: どこに住[す]んでいますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 家族と一緒に住みます。
example_sentences.english: I live together with my family.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[か]族[ぞく]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に住[す]みます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: High on the mountain trail, the lone vending machine will not open until the exact right coin drops in. That coin is the one thing <vocabulary>needed</vocabulary> to get a hot drink, and nothing else counts.
items.reading_mnemonic: An eel tossed onto the dry trail flaps in the dust, and a bucket of river water is the one thing it <vocabulary>needs</vocabulary> before it stops moving. It wheezes that demand as <reading>いる</reading>, almost the word <reading>eel</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 新しいペンが要る。
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しいペンが要[い]る。

example_sentences.japanese: お金は要りません。
example_sentences.furigana: お金[かね]は要[い]りません。

example_sentences.japanese: それ、要る？
example_sentences.furigana: それ、要[い]る？

items.meaning_mnemonic: The eye that does the <kanji>seeing</kanji> sprouts little legs, climbs a hill, and halts right out in the open. An eye that has stopped looking and turned into the thing anyone can look at is <vocabulary>to be visible</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 見 is read 「み」 from 見る, so this word for <vocabulary>to be visible</vocabulary> is simply <reading>みえる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 山が見えます。
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]が見[み]えます。

example_sentences.japanese: 夜、星が見える。
example_sentences.english: At night, the stars are visible.
example_sentences.furigana: 夜[よる]、星[ほし]が見[み]える。

example_sentences.japanese: 暗くて何も見えない。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Your ear is still jammed against that cold gate, but now the sounds push through the wood on their own. A noise that reaches you with no <kanji>hearing</kanji> on your part is <vocabulary>to be audible</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 聞 is read 「き」 from 聞く, so this word for <vocabulary>to be audible</vocabulary> is simply <reading>きこえる</reading>.

example_sentences.furigana: 窓[まど]から声[こえ]が聞[き]こえます。

example_sentences.japanese: ラジオが聞こえますか。
example_sentences.furigana: ラジオが聞[き]こえますか。

example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]の声[こえ]が聞[き]こえません。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the curry machine skips the whole queue and fires a hot pouch straight into your hands. Something that rams a packet at you unasked <vocabulary>gives</vocabulary> it to you, so say <reading>curry roo</reading> fast and you land on <reading>くれる</reading>.

example_sentences.english: My friend gives me a book.

example_sentences.japanese: 母がお菓子をくれました。

example_sentences.japanese: 誰がこれをくれる？

example_sentences.furigana: 誰[だれ]がこれをくれる？

items.meaning_mnemonic: A kangaroo has taken over the konbini till and keeps reaching into its pouch to <vocabulary>give out</vocabulary> a free onigiri to everyone in line. A <reading>kangaroo</reading> handing its whole pouch away, one item at a time, is <reading>あげる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 友達に本をあげます。
example_sentences.english: I'll give a book to my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]に本[ほん]をあげます。

example_sentences.english: My mom gave me some sweets.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は私[わたし]にお菓[か]子[し]をあげた。

example_sentences.japanese: これをあなたにあげます。
example_sentences.furigana: これをあなたにあげます。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your neighbour keeps lobbing enormous marrows over the riverbank fence for you to <vocabulary>receive</vocabulary>. Catching <reading>a marrow</reading> in both arms, day after day, is how you <reading>もらう</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 友達から本をもらう。
example_sentences.english: I get a book from my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]から本[ほん]をもらう。

example_sentences.japanese: 母からお菓子をもらった。
example_sentences.english: I got some sweets from my mom.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]からお菓[か]子[し]をもらった。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生にペンをもらいました。
example_sentences.english: I received a pen from my teacher.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]にペンをもらいました。

items.meaning: to be able to / be done
items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.

accepted_answers.answer_text: to be able to / be done

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's uncle brags that he will <vocabulary>be able to get a whole bare flat done</vocabulary> by lunch. A person who can <reading>deck a room</reading> that fast is one who <reading>できる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 料理ができます。
example_sentences.furigana: 料[りょう]理[り]ができます。

example_sentences.japanese: 晩ご飯ができました。
example_sentences.furigana: 晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]ができました。

example_sentences.japanese: ここで電話ができますか。
example_sentences.english: Can I make a phone call here?
example_sentences.furigana: ここで電[でん]話[わ]ができますか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Your keys should be in the front pocket, but your fingers close on <kanji>nothingness</kanji>. When a thing drops out of the world like that, you <vocabulary>lose</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Your keys should be in the front pocket of your <reading>knapsack</reading>, but your fingers close on nothing, <reading>なくす</reading>; they have dropped out of the world and you <vocabulary form="無くす">lose</vocabulary> them.

example_sentences.japanese: 財布を無くしました。
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]を無[な]くしました。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅で鍵を無くした。
example_sentences.english: I lost my keys at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]で鍵[かぎ]を無[な]くした。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は眼鏡を無くした。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は眼鏡[めがね]を無[な]くした。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The eye on legs that can <kanji>see</kanji> roams the world, checking everything it passes. When it stops because it has spotted the one thing it wanted, you <vocabulary>find</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met this 「み」 in 見る, to see, so the word for <vocabulary>to find</vocabulary> is simply <reading>みつける</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 鍵を見つけました。
example_sentences.furigana: 鍵[かぎ]を見[み]つけました。

example_sentences.japanese: どこでそれを見つけたの？
example_sentences.furigana: どこでそれを見[み]つけたの？

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、いい店を見つけた。
example_sentences.english: Yesterday I found a good shop.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、いい店[みせ]を見[み]つけた。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A parcel bound for another city and a friend boarding the last train get the very same treatment: you hand it over, then stand there watching it get smaller. That watching-it-leave is what it means to <vocabulary>send someone off</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every week the farmer mails a crate of <reading>okra</reading> to her sister and weeps on the platform as the train goes. The town decided that to <reading>おくる</reading> is to <vocabulary>send someone off</vocabulary> with your whole heart.

example_sentences.japanese: 友達に手紙を送る。
example_sentences.english: I send a letter to my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]に手[て]紙[がみ]を送[おく]る。

example_sentences.japanese: 空港まで友達を送る。
example_sentences.english: I see my friend off to the airport.
example_sentences.furigana: 空[くう]港[こう]まで友[とも]達[だち]を送[おく]る。

example_sentences.japanese: 母に写真を送った。
example_sentences.english: I sent a photo to my mom.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]に写[しゃ]真[しん]を送[おく]った。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A sack of rice on the ground is just furniture. Hoist it onto your shoulder and start walking, and now you <vocabulary>carry</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You hoist the rice sack onto one shoulder and <reading>half a coop</reading> of hens onto the other, <reading>はこぶ</reading>, and start walking: now you <vocabulary form="運ぶ">carry</vocabulary> it all.

example_sentences.japanese: この箱を運んでください。
example_sentences.furigana: この箱[はこ]を運[はこ]んでください。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と机を運ぶ。
example_sentences.english: I carry the desk with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と机[つくえ]を運[はこ]ぶ。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は野菜を家に運んだ。
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は野[や]菜[さい]を家[いえ]に運[はこ]んだ。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Ten identical umbrellas stand in the rack, and your hand can take only one. Picking that one and walking past the other nine is what it means to <vocabulary>choose</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: In the school shop Sei picks up and puts back every single <reading>rubber</reading> on the shelf until the bell finally rings. To <reading>えらぶ</reading> is to <vocabulary>choose</vocabulary> one and let the rest go.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はこの本を選びます。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はこの本[ほん]を選[えら]びます。

example_sentences.furigana: どれを選[えら]びますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は赤い服を選んだ。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は赤[あか]い服[ふく]を選[えら]んだ。

items.mnemonic_text: Hold it up to see: miseru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To <vocabulary>show</vocabulary> something is to shove it straight in front of another person's eyes so that they <kanji>see</kanji> it whether they wanted to or not.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 見 is 「み」 from 見る, so to <vocabulary>show</vocabulary> a thing by holding it up to the eyes is <reading>みせる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 写真を見せてください。
example_sentences.furigana: 写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]せてください。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は新しい本を見せた。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は新[あたら]しい本[ほん]を見[み]せた。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達にこれを見せます。

example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]にこれを見[み]せます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Shout a name across the room and the person turns; say it warmly with a date attached and they show up to dinner. Both are one verb: to <vocabulary>call or invite</vocabulary> someone.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi leans out the konbini door and shouts <reading>yo, boo</reading> at every regular he spots on the street. To <reading>よぶ</reading> is to <vocabulary>call someone over</vocabulary> until they come in.

example_sentences.japanese: 友達は私をケンと呼ぶ。
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]は私[わたし]をケンと呼[よ]ぶ。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日友達を呼びます。
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]友[とも]達[だち]を呼[よ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はタクシーを呼んだ。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]はタクシーを呼[よ]んだ。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You could pretend the wobbly stool is fine, but <kanji>honesty</kanji> makes you admit the leg is loose, so you set it straight again. Owning what is broken and putting it right is what it means <vocabulary>to fix / repair</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Honest Sue will not pretend the wobbly stool is fine: <reading>now, Sue</reading>, she tells herself, <reading>なおす</reading>, and she sets the loose leg straight to <vocabulary form="直す">fix</vocabulary> it.

example_sentences.japanese: 父が時計を直します。
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]が時計[とけい]を直[なお]します。

example_sentences.japanese: このドアを直した。
example_sentences.furigana: このドアを直[なお]した。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達がパソコンを直す。
example_sentences.english: My friend will fix the computer.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]がパソコンを直[なお]す。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Night drops on the mountain trail before you clear the ridge, and going down blind is how people get hurt. You take the bunk in the trail hut, boots by the door, and <vocabulary>stay overnight</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Boots by the door of the trail hut, you tell the dark ridge you will clear it <reading>tomorrow</reading>, <reading>とまる</reading>, and take the bunk to <vocabulary form="泊まる">stay overnight</vocabulary>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The only way up to the tree house is the knotted rope, hand over hand, feet slipping on bark. Hauling yourself up something steep like that, using your whole body, is what it means <vocabulary>to climb</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>No bull</reading> could get up the knotted rope to the tree house, but you go hand over hand, feet slipping on bark, <reading>のぼる</reading>, to <vocabulary form="登る">climb</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は山[やま]に登[のぼ]ります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Your ring slips off at the riverbank and vanishes into the reeds, so now you are on your knees parting every stalk. Going over a place inch by inch after one lost thing is what it means <vocabulary>to search for</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: On your knees at the riverbank, parting every reed for your lost ring, you mutter that this will take longer than the old Norse <reading>sagas</reading>, <reading>さがす</reading>; that is to <vocabulary form="探す">search for</vocabulary> it.

example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]で鍵[かぎ]を探[さが]す。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅で友達を探します。
example_sentences.english: I'll look for my friend at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]で友[とも]達[だち]を探[さが]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日財布を探した。
example_sentences.english: Yesterday I searched for my wallet.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]財[さい]布[ふ]を探[さが]した。

items.mnemonic_text: Set them in a row: naraberu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take a shelf of jumbled cans and turn every label to face front, one behind the next, until they make a clean <kanji>row</kanji>. Setting objects out in a straight rank like that, by hand, is what it means <vocabulary>to line them up</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Night clerk <reading>Nara Bell</reading> turns every jumbled can on the shelf label-out, one behind the next, humming 「<reading>ならべる</reading>」 because her whole job is <vocabulary form="並べる">to line up</vocabulary> the cans.

example_sentences.japanese: 本を机に並べる。
example_sentences.english: I line up the books on the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]を机[つくえ]に並[なら]べる。

example_sentences.japanese: 母が野菜を並べます。
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]が野[や]菜[さい]を並[なら]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: 子供が椅子を並べた。
example_sentences.english: The child lined up the chairs.
example_sentences.furigana: 子[こ]供[ども]が椅[い]子[す]を並[なら]べた。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>walk along</kanji> a message, carrying it down a line of people one hand to the next, until it reaches the far end. Passing something all the way down the line is what it means <vocabulary>to convey / tell</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>two-tailer</reading> lizard courier sprints between houses, flicking one tail per word so the next house gets the message. A tail-flicked relay like that is what it means <vocabulary>to convey / tell</vocabulary>, and its name is 「<reading>つたえる</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼にこれを伝えます。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]にこれを伝[つた]えます。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生に伝えてください。
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]に伝[つた]えてください。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女に好きだと伝えた。
example_sentences.english: I told her that I like her.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]に好[す]きだと伝[つた]えた。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Call a question into the school's empty, echoing hallway and just wait. The reply that comes bouncing back on its own, with nobody standing there to give it, is the hall beginning <vocabulary>to answer</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The kangaroo mascot <reading>Cot-a-roo</reading> hops down the empty school hallway; yell a question at it and the hall bounces back 「<reading>こたえる</reading>」, as if the walls had learned <vocabulary form="答える">to answer</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生に答えます。
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]に答[こた]えます。

example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は丁[てい]寧[ねい]に答[こた]えました。

example_sentences.japanese: 何と答えますか。
example_sentences.furigana: 何[なに]と答[こた]えますか。

items.word_type: する verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 質（しつ）＋問（もん）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Walk up to the shouting gate at the school and throw its own <kanji>question</kanji> straight back through the bars at it. Flinging a question at something to force it to talk is what it is <vocabulary>to ask a question</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は先生に質問する。
example_sentences.english: I ask the teacher a question.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は先[せん]生[せい]に質[しつ]問[もん]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 何を質問する？
example_sentences.furigana: 何[なに]を質[しつ]問[もん]する？

example_sentences.japanese: 学生が先生に質問する。
example_sentences.english: The student asks the teacher a question.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]が先[せん]生[せい]に質[しつ]問[もん]する。

items.word_type: する verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 電（でん）＋話（わ）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Pour your nonstop <kanji>talk</kanji> into the wire and let the house current's caught <kanji>electricity</kanji> shove it clear across town to someone's ear. Driving your words down a live line like that is what it is <vocabulary>to phone</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]、母[はは]に電[でん]話[わ]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、友達に電話する。
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]に電[でん]話[わ]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は毎晩彼女に電話する。
example_sentences.english: He phones his girlfriend every night.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は毎[まい]晩[ばん]彼[かの]女[じょ]に電[でん]話[わ]する。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 旅（りょ）＋行（こう）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Shoulder your pack for a <kanji>trip</kanji> and keep choosing to <kanji>go</kanji> at every crossroads, one town after the next. Staying on the move like that, wherever the road forks, is what it is <vocabulary>to travel</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.english: Next month I'll travel with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]月[げつ]、友[とも]達[だち]と旅[りょ]行[こう]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末に旅行するのが好きです。

example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]に旅[りょ]行[こう]するのが好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 家族と旅行する暇がない。
example_sentences.english: I have no free time to travel with my family.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[か]族[ぞく]と旅[りょ]行[こう]する暇[ひま]がない。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 買（か）＋い＋物（もの）＋する.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You throw a net over one <kanji>thing</kanji> after another and drop clam-shell coins on the counter to <kanji>buy</kanji> each one. Keep that up stall after stall and you are out to <vocabulary>shop</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日スーパーで買い物する。
example_sentences.english: I shop at the supermarket today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]スーパーで買[か]い物[もの]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 母と一緒に買い物する。
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に買[か]い物[もの]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末デパートで買い物する。
example_sentences.english: I shop at the department store on weekends.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]デパートで買[か]い物[もの]する。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 散（さん）＋歩（ぽ）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi. Handakuon: 歩 ほ → ぽ.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your feet stop flat every few steps and the path just <kanji>scatters</kanji> wherever it likes, aiming nowhere. A <kanji>walk</kanji> that loose and unplanned is you choosing to <vocabulary>take a walk</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 父は毎朝散歩する。
example_sentences.english: My father takes a walk every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]散[さん]歩[ぽ]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は夜散歩するのが好きです。
example_sentences.english: I like taking walks at night.
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は夜[よる]散[さん]歩[ぽ]するのが好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女と一緒に散歩する。
example_sentences.english: I take a walk with her.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に散[さん]歩[ぽ]する。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 掃（そう）＋除（じ）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Tidy it all up: souji suru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: First you <kanji>sweep</kanji> every crumb into one pile, then you <kanji>remove</kanji> it from the floor for good. Do both, and the room is <vocabulary>clean</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日部屋を掃除する。
example_sentences.english: I clean my room every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]部屋[へや]を掃[そう]除[じ]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 母が台所を掃除する。
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]が台[だい]所[どころ]を掃[そう]除[じ]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 一緒にトイレを掃除する。
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いっ]緒[しょ]にトイレを掃[そう]除[じ]する。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 洗（せん）＋濯（たく）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>wash</kanji> here is not the dishes and not your hands, but a heaped basket of dirty shirts and socks. That one narrowed-down job is exactly what it means to <vocabulary>do laundry</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、服を洗濯する。
example_sentences.english: I'll do laundry for my clothes today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、服[ふく]を洗[せん]濯[たく]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は毎朝洗濯する。
example_sentences.english: My mother does laundry every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]洗[せん]濯[たく]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 汚いシャツを洗濯する。
example_sentences.furigana: 汚[きたな]いシャツを洗[せん]濯[たく]する。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 料（りょう）＋理（り）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You take raw <kanji>materials</kanji> and run them through the strict <kanji>logic</kanji> of a recipe, step after step. When that turns them into a hot meal, you <vocabulary>cook</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 母は台所で料理する。
example_sentences.english: My mother cooks in the kitchen.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は台[だい]所[どころ]で料[りょう]理[り]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は魚を料理する。
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は魚[さかな]を料[りょう]理[り]する。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は料理するのが好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は料[りょう]理[り]するのが好[す]きです。

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 仕（し）on'yomi ＋ 事（ごと）kun'yomi. Rendaku: 事 こと → ごと.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>matter</kanji> you loyally <kanji>attend</kanji> to day after day, sandals fetched and tea poured, is your <vocabulary>work / job</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は仕事があります。
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は仕[し]事[ごと]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: この仕事は難しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: この仕[し]事[ごと]は難[むずか]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は仕事を休みます。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow I'm taking the day off work.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は仕[し]事[ごと]を休[やす]みます。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 授（じゅ）＋業（ぎょう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A set hour in which a teacher will <kanji>impart</kanji> the skills of a trade or <kanji>business</kanji> to you is a <vocabulary>class / lesson</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は授業があります。
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 授業は何時に始まりますか。
example_sentences.furigana: 授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]は何[なん]時[じ]に始[はじ]まりますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は授業を休みました。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]を休[やす]みました。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 宿（しゅく）＋題（だい）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>topic</kanji> from class that follows you home to your <kanji>lodging</kanji> and demands work before morning is <vocabulary>homework</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日の宿題を忘れました。
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]の宿[しゅく]題[だい]を忘[わす]れました。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は宿題をしません。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother doesn't do his homework.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしません。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は宿題を出します。
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は宿[しゅく]題[だい]を出[だ]します。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 試（し）＋験（けん）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A single formal <kanji>try</kanji> that the school scores, records, and later holds against your name is an <vocabulary>exam</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 来週は試験です。
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]は試[し]験[けん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: この試験は難しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: この試[し]験[けん]は難[むずか]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、学校で試験があります。
example_sentences.english: There's an exam at school tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、学[がっ]校[こう]で試[し]験[けん]があります。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Tess never revises, so the pop quiz lands, she panics, kicks the desk leg, and jams her <reading>Tess toe</reading>. Her yelp of <reading>テスト</reading> is the sound of every surprise <vocabulary>test</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日はテストがあります。
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]はテストがあります。

example_sentences.japanese: このテストは難しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: このテストは難[むずか]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生はテストを出しました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher handed out a test.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]はテストを出[だ]しました。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 勉（べん）＋強（きょう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Pour in enough <kanji>exertion</kanji> to build a <kanji>strong</kanji> hold on a subject, sweatband wrung dry, and that grind is <vocabulary>study</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 勉強は難しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 勉[べん]強[きょう]は難[むずか]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝勉強をします。
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]勉[べん]強[きょう]をします。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は勉強が好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は勉[べん]強[きょう]が好[す]きです。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 問（もん）＋題（だい）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>question</kanji> set as the <kanji>topic</kanji> at the top of a worksheet, waiting for you to crack it, is a <vocabulary>problem / question</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 大きな問題があります。
example_sentences.furigana: 大[おお]きな問[もん]題[だい]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: この問題に答えます。
example_sentences.furigana: この問[もん]題[だい]に答[こた]えます。

example_sentences.japanese: 試験の問題は難しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 試[し]験[けん]の問[もん]題[だい]は難[むずか]しいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The hand that shoots up, the words that make the teacher stop scanning the room and nod, is the <vocabulary>answer</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 答 is 「こた」 from 答える, so the <vocabulary>answer</vocabulary> you fill the blank with is <reading>こたえ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 答えはこれです。
example_sentences.furigana: 答[こた]えはこれです。

example_sentences.japanese: 難しい答えを書きました。
example_sentences.furigana: 難[むずか]しい答[こた]えを書[か]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 答えが分かりません。
example_sentences.furigana: 答[こた]えが分[わ]かりません。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 意（い）＋味（み）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>idea</kanji> you can almost <kanji>taste</kanji> when a word is used just right is that word's <vocabulary>meaning</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この問題の意味が分かりません。
example_sentences.english: I don't understand what this question means.
example_sentences.furigana: この問[もん]題[だい]の意[い]味[み]が分[わ]かりません。

example_sentences.japanese: その意味を教えてください。
example_sentences.english: Please tell me what that means.
example_sentences.furigana: その意[い]味[み]を教[おし]えてください。

example_sentences.japanese: 何の意味ですか。
example_sentences.furigana: 何[なに]の意[い]味[み]ですか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 言（こと）＋葉（ば）. Rendaku: 葉 は → ば.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Each <kanji>leaf</kanji> on the tree is one thing a person once chose to <kanji>say</kanji>, and the whole crown of them together is <vocabulary>language</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この言葉の意味が分かりません。
example_sentences.english: I don't understand the meaning of this word.
example_sentences.furigana: この言[こと]葉[ば]の意[い]味[み]が分[わ]かりません。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は新しい言葉を教えます。
example_sentences.english: The teacher teaches a new word.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は新[あたら]しい言[こと]葉[ば]を教[おし]えます。

example_sentences.japanese: 難しい言葉を忘れました。
example_sentences.furigana: 難[むずか]しい言[こと]葉[ば]を忘[わす]れました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The evening hides your face, so your <kanji>name</kanji> is the one word you send out in <kanji>front</kanji> of you. A word carried ahead like that, so strangers know who just spoke, is your <vocabulary>name</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の名前はユキです。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の名[な]前[まえ]はユキです。

example_sentences.japanese: あなたの名前は何ですか。
example_sentences.furigana: あなたの名[な]前[まえ]は何[なに]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼の名前を忘れました。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]の名[な]前[まえ]を忘[わす]れました。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 漢（かん）＋字（じ）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A written <kanji>character</kanji> that walked over from <kanji>China</kanji> and settled in Japan for good is a <vocabulary>kanji</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この漢字は難しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: この漢[かん]字[じ]は難[むずか]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日漢字を勉強します。
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]漢[かん]字[じ]を勉[べん]強[きょう]します。

example_sentences.japanese: ノートに漢字を書きます。
example_sentences.english: I write kanji in my notebook.
example_sentences.furigana: ノートに漢[かん]字[じ]を書[か]きます。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Rumor goes that <reading>Hera gonna</reading> teach the soft, looping letters first, before anything with a sharp edge, and that rounded beginner script is <vocabulary>hiragana</vocabulary>. Say the goddess and her plan in one breath and you land on <reading>ひらがな</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はひらがなを書けます。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はひらがなを書[か]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: ひらがなは読めますか。
example_sentences.furigana: ひらがなは読[よ]めますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日ひらがなを勉強します。
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]ひらがなを勉[べん]強[きょう]します。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The letters look like someone took a ruler and decided to <reading>cut a corner</reading> on every curve, leaving nothing but sharp straight angles. That stiff script for foreign words is <vocabulary>katakana</vocabulary>, and <reading>カタカナ</reading> is that phrase said fast.

example_sentences.japanese: ノートにカタカナを書きます。
example_sentences.english: I write katakana in my notebook.
example_sentences.furigana: ノートにカタカナを書[か]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: カタカナは難しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: カタカナは難[むずか]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: ひらがなとカタカナを覚えます。
example_sentences.furigana: ひらがなとカタカナを覚[おぼ]えます。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 英（えい）＋語（ご）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hold one <kanji>language</kanji> under a waterfall of foreign words, let it swallow every one whole, and never let it spit a single word back. What pours out the bottom is <vocabulary>English</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 鈴木先生は英語を教えます。
example_sentences.furigana: 鈴木[すずき]先[せん]生[せい]は英[えい]語[ご]を教[おし]えます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は毎日英語を勉強しています。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は毎[まい]日[にち]英[えい]語[ご]を勉[べん]強[きょう]しています。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は英語が分かります。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は英[えい]語[ご]が分[わ]かります。

items.reading_composition: Irregular — にほんご cannot be assembled from the dictionary readings of 日本語.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sun</kanji> rises first over the land at the <kanji>origin</kanji> of the day. The <kanji>language</kanji> they speak there is <vocabulary>Japanese</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: As the sun rises first over that land, a goose on the shore greets it with a loud <reading>knee-honk-go</reading>, the day's first word of <vocabulary form="日本語">Japanese</vocabulary>: 「<reading>にほんご</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日日本語を勉強します。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]日本[にほん]語[ご]を勉[べん]強[きょう]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は日本語で話しました。
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は日本[にほん]語[ご]で話[はな]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は日本語が上手です。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は日本[にほん]語[ご]が上手[じょうず]です。

items.reading_composition: Irregular — にほん cannot be assembled from the dictionary readings of 日本.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sun</kanji> clears the horizon here first, at the very <kanji>origin</kanji> of the day. That country is <vocabulary>Japan</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker at the top of the mountain trail watches the sunrise and raps her <reading>knee bone</reading> twice for the beats as she names the country it rises over, 「<reading>にほん</reading>」, and that country is <vocabulary>Japan</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は日本が好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は日本[にほん]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄は日本に住んでいます。
example_sentences.english: My older brother lives in Japan.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]は日本[にほん]に住[す]んでいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 日本の食べ物はおいしいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 日本[にほん]の食[た]べ物[もの]はおいしいです。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 外（がい）＋国（こく）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>country</kanji> is walls thrown up around the one jewel its people will not share. Any such enclosure <kanji>outside</kanji> your own is a <vocabulary>foreign country</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は外国に住みたいです。
example_sentences.english: I want to live in a foreign country.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は外[がい]国[こく]に住[す]みたいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は外国で日本語を教えました。
example_sentences.english: She taught Japanese in a foreign country.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は外[がい]国[こく]で日本[にほん]語[ご]を教[おし]えました。

example_sentences.japanese: 来年、外国へ旅行します。
example_sentences.english: Next year, I'll travel to a foreign country.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]、外[がい]国[こく]へ旅[りょ]行[こう]します。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 会（かい）＋議（ぎ）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Trap eight people around one table in slow formal <kanji>deliberation</kanji>, refill the coffee twice, and what you are left with is a <vocabulary>meeting</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日会議があります。
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]会[かい]議[ぎ]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は会議で話しました。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は会[かい]議[ぎ]で話[はな]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日の会議は長かったです。
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]の会[かい]議[ぎ]は長[なが]かったです。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 約（やく）＋束（そく）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary>promise / appointment</vocabulary> is a <kanji>bundle</kanji> of your own future hours. You tie it shut and hand it to someone else to hold.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女と会う約束をしました。
example_sentences.english: I made a promise to meet her.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]と会[あ]う約[やく]束[そく]をしました。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、彼と約束があります。
example_sentences.english: I have an appointment with him tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、彼[かれ]と約[やく]束[そく]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達との約束を忘れました。
example_sentences.english: I forgot my promise with my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]との約[やく]束[そく]を忘[わす]れました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>money</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>money</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane keeps her gold coins in a little roofed safe, and when she lifts the lid, visitors gasp '<reading>oh, Kane</reading>' at so much <vocabulary form="お金">money</vocabulary>: 「<reading>おかね</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: 財布にお金がありません。
example_sentences.english: There's no money in my wallet.
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]にお金[かね]がありません。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達にお金を借りました。
example_sentences.english: I borrowed money from a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]にお金[かね]を借[か]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行でお金を払います。
example_sentences.english: I'll pay the money at the bank.
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]でお金[かね]を払[はら]います。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 旅（りょ）＋行（こう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>trip</kanji> stays a daydream until the two of you follow the banner to the crossroads and actually <kanji>go</kanji>. Once your feet move, that is <vocabulary>trip / travel</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 旅行は楽しかったです。
example_sentences.furigana: 旅[りょ]行[こう]は楽[たの]しかったです。

example_sentences.japanese: 来年家族と旅行に行きます。
example_sentences.english: Next year I'll go on a trip with my family.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]家[か]族[ぞく]と旅[りょ]行[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達との旅行は楽しいです。
example_sentences.english: A trip with a friend is fun.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]との旅[りょ]行[こう]は楽[たの]しいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You sling your net over stall after stall and drop a shell on each counter to <kanji>buy</kanji> every <kanji>thing</kanji> that is not nailed down. Hauling that catch home is <vocabulary>shopping</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は友達と買い物に行きます。
example_sentences.english: Today I'm going shopping with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は友[とも]達[だち]と買[か]い物[もの]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日デパートで買い物をしました。
example_sentences.english: I did some shopping at the department store yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]デパートで買[か]い物[もの]をしました。

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は買い物が好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は買[か]い物[もの]が好[す]きです。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The school field's mascot is an old whale in a tank who <reading>spouts</reading> once for every point scored, so the team has taken to calling the whole match 「<reading>スポーツ</reading>」, their word for <vocabulary>sports</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はスポーツが好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はスポーツが好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は毎週スポーツをします。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother does sports every week.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は毎[まい]週[しゅう]スポーツをします。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はどんなスポーツも上手です。
example_sentences.english: He's good at every kind of sport.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]はどんなスポーツも上手[じょうず]です。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 音（おん）＋楽（がく）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take the kind of <kanji>sound</kanji> that makes you sit up in a silent room and string it along a branch like ice beads until sitting and listening is pure <kanji>comfort</kanji>. That is <vocabulary>music</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は音楽が好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は音[おん]楽[がく]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は毎朝音楽を聞きます。
example_sentences.english: She listens to music every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]音[おん]楽[がく]を聞[き]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: この音楽は面白いですね。
example_sentences.english: This music is interesting, isn't it.
example_sentences.furigana: この音[おん]楽[がく]は面[おも]白[しろ]いですね。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 映（えい）＋画（が）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Stack up a pile of <kanji>pictures</kanji> and <kanji>reflect</kanji> them onto a white wall one after another, fast. The moving image on the wall is a <vocabulary>movie</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は映画が好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は映[えい]画[が]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow I'll watch a movie with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: その映画は面白かったです。
example_sentences.furigana: その映[えい]画[が]は面白[おもしろ]かったです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Words turn into a <vocabulary>song</vocabulary> the moment a tune picks them up and makes them rise and fall instead of lying flat.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met this reading in 歌う, so a <vocabulary>song</vocabulary> is just <reading>うた</reading> again.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はいつも楽しい歌を歌います。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はいつも楽[たの]しい歌[うた]を歌[うた]います。

example_sentences.japanese: この歌は好きですか。
example_sentences.furigana: この歌[うた]は好[す]きですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と一緒に歌を歌いました。
example_sentences.english: I sang a song together with my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に歌[うた]を歌[うた]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A kid scribbles crayon over a whole page until the blob is unmistakably the family dog. Any marks made to stand for a real thing are a <vocabulary>drawing</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 娘は絵が好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 娘[むすめ]は絵[え]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は部屋で絵を見ました。
example_sentences.english: He looked at a picture in the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は部屋[へや]で絵[え]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: この絵は古いです。
example_sentences.furigana: この絵[え]は古[ふる]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>talk</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>story</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they carry the very same meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: A parrot on the riverbank has memorised exactly one rambling <vocabulary>story</vocabulary> and retells it to every heron that lands, squawking <reading>はなし</reading> like <reading>'her Nashi pear'</reading> at the same spot each time.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はよく友達と話します。
example_sentences.english: I often talk with my friends.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はよく友[とも]達[だち]と話[はな]します。

example_sentences.japanese: その話は面白いですか？
example_sentences.furigana: その話[はなし]は面[おも]白[しろ]いですか？

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は昨日、面白い話をしました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher told an interesting story yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は昨日[きのう]、面[おも]白[しろ]い話[はなし]をしました。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 質（しつ）＋問（もん）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school the gate won't open until you answer the <kanji>question</kanji> shouted through its bars. Take that same demand for an answer indoors, hand raised, and you are asking a <vocabulary>question</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は先生に質問しました。
example_sentences.english: I asked the teacher a question.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は先[せん]生[せい]に質[しつ]問[もん]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: その質問は難しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: その質[しつ]問[もん]は難[むずか]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は授業で質問をしました。
example_sentences.english: She asked a question during class.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]で質[しつ]問[もん]をしました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>thing</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>thing (object)</vocabulary> word are exactly the same character, and they point at the same idea, a plain object and nothing more.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the farm the cow gets a sweet name, but the farmer calls every bucket and fork in one flat <reading>monotone</reading>: 「<reading>もの</reading>」, just a <vocabulary form="物">thing</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: これは私の物です。
example_sentences.furigana: これは私[わたし]の物[もの]です。

example_sentences.japanese: その箱の物は何ですか。
example_sentences.english: What are the things in that box?
example_sentences.furigana: その箱[はこ]の物[もの]は何[なに]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: その物を取ってください。
example_sentences.furigana: その物[もの]を取[と]ってください。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the shrine a lantern tips over and an offering goes missing the same morning. Grandma Kane writes each mishap on a slip and calls it one more <vocabulary>thing (matter)</vocabulary> to deal with.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane winds a <reading>cotton</reading> string round her finger for every unfinished <vocabulary>thing (matter)</vocabulary> on her mind. By noon her hand is a fat white ball she taps while muttering 「<reading>こと</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の言う事を聞いてください。
example_sentences.english: Please listen to what I say.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の言[い]う事[こと]を聞[き]いてください。

example_sentences.japanese: それは面白い事ですね。
example_sentences.english: That's an interesting thing, isn't it.
example_sentences.furigana: それは面[おも]白[しろ]い事[こと]ですね。

example_sentences.japanese: 好きな事をしました。
example_sentences.furigana: 好[す]きな事[こと]をしました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker on the mountain trail keeps one photo taped inside his hat. It marks the exact <vocabulary>place</vocabulary> where the path forks to the vending machine, and missing the fork costs him an hour back down.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the fork the hiker taps the photo in his hat and groans '<reading>took a road</reading> wrong here once,' so 「<reading>ところ</reading>」 marks the exact <vocabulary form="所">place</vocabulary> the path splits to the vending machine.

example_sentences.japanese: ここは静かな所です。
example_sentences.furigana: ここは静[しず]かな所[ところ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は静かな所が好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は静[しず]かな所[ところ]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: あそこは有名な所です。
example_sentences.english: That place over there is famous.
example_sentences.furigana: あそこは有[ゆう]名[めい]な所[ところ]です。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The wooden signpost at the riverbank has spun loose on its post. Now every one of its four arrows points the same <vocabulary>direction / way</vocabulary>, and travellers stand there bickering over which arrow to trust.

example_sentences.japanese: すみません、駅はどちらの方ですか。
example_sentences.english: Excuse me, which way is the station?
example_sentences.furigana: すみません、駅[えき]はどちらの方[ほう]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 郵便局はあちらの方です。
example_sentences.english: The post office is that way.
example_sentences.furigana: 郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]はあちらの方[ほう]です。

example_sentences.japanese: こちらの方が近いです。
example_sentences.furigana: こちらの方[ほう]が近[ちか]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The new receptionist at the school is painfully formal. She greets every student, even the smallest, as an honoured <vocabulary>person (polite)</vocabulary>, bowing before she hands back a dropped pencil.
items.reading_mnemonic: The receptionist summons the school's gruff hedge <reading>cutter</reading> to shape the entrance bushes. Even he is welcomed as an honoured <vocabulary>person (polite)</vocabulary>, with a deep bow and a careful 「<reading>かた</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: あの方は先生です。
example_sentences.english: That person over there is a teacher.
example_sentences.furigana: あの方[ほう]は先[せん]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: この方は誰ですか。
example_sentences.furigana: この方[ほう]は誰[だれ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: その方はとても親切でした。
example_sentences.furigana: その方[ほう]はとても親[しん]切[せつ]でした。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>between</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>between</vocabulary> word are the same character with the same meaning, so there is nothing new to learn here.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kids at the open gate dare each other, '<reading>I dare</reading> you,' to step into the sliver of low sun caught <vocabulary form="間">between</vocabulary> the two doors: 「<reading>あいだ</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: 授業の間、静かに座っていました。
example_sentences.furigana: 授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]の間[あいだ]、静[しず]かに座[すわ]っていました。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達を待っている間に、コーヒーを飲みました。
example_sentences.english: While I was waiting for my friend, I drank some coffee.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]を待[ま]っている間[あいだ]に、コーヒーを飲[の]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: 朝と晩の間に、宿題をしました。
example_sentences.english: I did my homework sometime between morning and evening.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]と晩[ばん]の間[あいだ]に、宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>near</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>nearby</vocabulary> word are the same, so they mean the same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 近 is 「ちか」 from 近い, so <vocabulary>nearby</vocabulary> is <reading>ちかく</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の近くに図書館があります。
example_sentences.english: There's a library near the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の近[ちか]くに図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の家はこの近くです。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の家[いえ]はこの近[ちか]くです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は公園の近くに住んでいます。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は公[こう]園[えん]の近[ちか]くに住[す]んでいます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The house sharing your wall is so close you hear its radio through the plaster and its cat scratches at your door. That wall-to-wall closeness is your <vocabulary>neighbor</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every noon the cat from the house sharing your wall scratches at your door for a bite of your <reading>tuna rye</reading>, 「<reading>となり</reading>」, the lunch that keeps your <vocabulary form="隣">neighbor</vocabulary> close.

example_sentences.japanese: 隣に猫がいます。
example_sentences.english: There's a cat next to me.
example_sentences.furigana: 隣[となり]に猫[ねこ]がいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 隣の部屋は静かです。
example_sentences.english: The room next door is quiet.
example_sentences.furigana: 隣[となり]の部屋[へや]は静[しず]かです。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の隣に座ってください。
example_sentences.english: Please sit down next to me.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の隣[となり]に座[すわ]ってください。

items.meaning_mnemonic: This word is just the <kanji>behind</kanji> kanji you already know, so <vocabulary>behind</vocabulary> is exactly what it means.
items.reading_mnemonic: '<reading>Ooh, she rowed</reading>!' cry the fans as a duck paddles hard with a tiny thread caught on her trailing foot, yet that foot still lands a beat <vocabulary form="後ろ">behind</vocabulary>: 「<reading>うしろ</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: 後ろに猫がいます。
example_sentences.furigana: 後[うし]ろに猫[ねこ]がいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は私の後ろに立ちました。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は私[わたし]の後[うし]ろに立[た]ちました。

example_sentences.japanese: かばんは椅子の後ろにありました。
example_sentences.english: The bag was behind the chair.
example_sentences.furigana: かばんは椅[い]子[す]の後[うし]ろにありました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>front</kanji> kanji standing on its own is the <vocabulary>front</vocabulary> word, meaning and all.
items.reading_mnemonic: Farmhand <reading>Mae</reading> crosses the moonlit yard and freezes right in <vocabulary form="前">front</vocabulary> of the cow guarding its dropped knife, whispering her own name, 「<reading>まえ</reading>」, to calm it.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の前でともだちを待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I'll wait for my friend in front of the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の前[まえ]でともだちを待[ま]ちます。

example_sentences.japanese: 食事の前に手を洗います。
example_sentences.english: I wash my hands before meals.
example_sentences.furigana: 食[しょく]事[じ]の前[まえ]に手[て]を洗[あら]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 三日前、私はこの町に来ました。
example_sentences.english: Three days ago, I came to this town.
example_sentences.furigana: 三[みっ]日[か]前[まえ]、私[わたし]はこの町[まち]に来[き]ました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Written alone, the <kanji>inside</kanji> kanji is simply the word for <vocabulary>inside</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Shove the stick through the wide mouth until it stops dead in the <vocabulary form="中">middle</vocabulary>, then <reading>knock a</reading> knuckle on it, and whatever is pinned in there squeaks 「<reading>なか</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: 箱の中に猫がいます。
example_sentences.english: There's a cat inside the box.
example_sentences.furigana: 箱[はこ]の中[なか]に猫[ねこ]がいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋の中は暗かったです。
example_sentences.english: The inside of the room was dark.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]の中[なか]は暗[くら]かったです。

example_sentences.japanese: かばんの中に財布がありました。
example_sentences.english: There was a wallet inside the bag.
example_sentences.furigana: かばんの中[なか]に財[さい]布[ふ]がありました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>outside</kanji> kanji by itself is the <vocabulary>outside</vocabulary> word, unchanged in meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: Shuffling <vocabulary form="外">outside</vocabulary> to catch the last evening sun, the divining tortoise stubs its toe on the step and grumbles '<reading>so, toe</reading>,' 「<reading>そと</reading>」, before reading its cracked shell.

example_sentences.japanese: 外は寒いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 外[そと]は寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬は外にいます。
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]は外[そと]にいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 外で遊びましょう。
example_sentences.furigana: 外[そと]で遊[あそ]びましょう。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Standing by itself, the <kanji>up</kanji> kanji is just the <vocabulary>up</vocabulary> word, nothing added.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mossy shrine steps, a monk follows the tortoise's crack from the ground line and gasps '<reading>ooh, eh?</reading>' at where it points: 「<reading>うえ</reading>」, straight <vocabulary form="上">up</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 本は机の上にあります。
example_sentences.english: The book is on the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]は机[つくえ]の上[うえ]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫は木の上にいます。
example_sentences.english: The cat is up in the tree.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]は木[き]の上[うえ]にいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 山の上は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It's cold at the top of the mountain.
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]の上[うえ]は寒[さむ]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: This is just the <kanji>down</kanji> kanji you have met, used on its own as the word <vocabulary>down</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Under the ground line, a <reading>cheetah</reading> crouches in the dark and bats at the divination mark dangling <vocabulary form="下">down</vocabulary> to it, purring 「<reading>した</reading>」 since nobody above ever reads it.

example_sentences.japanese: 猫はテーブルの下で寝ています。
example_sentences.english: The cat is sleeping under the table.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]はテーブルの下[した]で寝[ね]ています。

example_sentences.japanese: 財布を椅子の下で見つけました。
example_sentences.english: I found my wallet under the chair.
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]を椅[い]子[す]の下[した]で見[み]つけました。

example_sentences.japanese: 山の下に川があります。
example_sentences.english: There is a river below the mountain.
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]の下[した]に川[かわ]があります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: On its own, the <kanji>right</kanji> kanji is exactly the <vocabulary>right</vocabulary> word, no more and no less.
items.reading_mnemonic: With her left hand busy holding the rice bowl, <reading>Miggy</reading> the mongoose shovels every bite to her mouth with her <vocabulary form="右">right</vocabulary>, chattering 「<reading>みぎ</reading>」 between mouthfuls.

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行は右にあります。
example_sentences.english: The bank is on the right.
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]は右[みぎ]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 右の目が痛いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 右[みぎ]の目[め]が痛[いた]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: あの角を右に曲がってください。
example_sentences.english: Please turn right at that corner.
example_sentences.furigana: あの角[かど]を右[みぎ]に曲[ま]がってください。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>left</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>left</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they carry the very same meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: A builder <reading>hid a ring</reading> in the glove of the hand that only braces the girder while the other one bolts, so 「<reading>ひだり</reading>」, his <vocabulary form="左">left</vocabulary>, never moves enough to lose it.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は角で左に曲がりました。
example_sentences.english: He turned left at the corner.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は角[かど]で左[ひだり]に曲[ま]がりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行はデパートの左にあります。
example_sentences.english: The bank is to the left of the department store.
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]はデパートの左[ひだり]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 左の目が痛いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 左[ひだり]の目[め]が痛[いた]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: Backs turned to the cold: kita.
items.meaning_mnemonic: This word is just the <kanji>north</kanji> kanji standing on its own, so the <vocabulary>north</vocabulary> word means exactly what the kanji does.
items.reading_mnemonic: Two campers sit back to back against the cold wind from the <vocabulary form="北">north</vocabulary>, and the one called <reading>Keeta</reading> shouts 「<reading>きた</reading>」 at it to make it stop.

example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]の方[ほう]に大[おお]きい山[やま]があります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>south</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>south</vocabulary> word are one and the same, with nothing added and nothing changed.
items.reading_mnemonic: Two horns poke out of the box lashed to the one warm, dry wall, where the goat inside basks as if in <reading>Miami</reading>, 「<reading>みなみ</reading>」, because that wall faces <vocabulary form="南">south</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 南はあちらです。
example_sentences.furigana: 南[みなみ]はあちらです。

example_sentences.japanese: 冬でも南は暖かいです。
example_sentences.english: Even in winter, the south is warm.
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]でも南[みなみ]は暖[あたた]かいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Written on its own, the <kanji>east</kanji> kanji is already the whole <vocabulary>east</vocabulary> word, and the meaning does not shift at all.
items.reading_mnemonic: At dawn the sun forces a <reading>big gash</reading> of light through the <vocabulary>east</vocabulary> horizon. Hear that tearing sound and you are saying <reading>ひがし</reading>.

example_sentences.furigana: あの山[やま]は東[ひがし]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 東の空に月が見えます。
example_sentences.english: The moon can be seen in the eastern sky.
example_sentences.furigana: 東[ひがし]の空[そら]に月[つき]が見[み]えます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>west</kanji> kanji is the entire <vocabulary>west</vocabulary> word by itself, so the two mean precisely the same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every evening the sinking sun burns a glowing <reading>niche</reading> into the <vocabulary>west</vocabulary> wall of the shrine. The cats curl into that <reading>にし</reading>-shaped alcove for the last of the warmth.

example_sentences.japanese: 山は西のほうにあります。
example_sentences.english: The mountain is in the western direction.
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]は西[にし]のほうにあります。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 半（はん）＋分（ぶん）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>half</kanji> only counts as a real <vocabulary>half</vocabulary> once it is also a clean <kanji>part</kanji> you can lift away and hand to someone.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 全（ぜん）＋部（ぶ）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Pull together every single <kanji>section</kanji> of a thing, skip none, and what is left in your hands is the <vocabulary>whole</vocabulary> of it.

example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]を全[ぜん]部[ぶ]読[よ]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: 全部おいしかったです。
example_sentences.furigana: 全[ぜん]部[ぶ]おいしかったです。

items.word_type: な adjective, adverb, noun, の adjective
items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A kid at the crossing counts cab after cab and loses count; "that's <reading>taxi, son</reading>," his grandfather says, meaning <reading>たくさん</reading>, <vocabulary>a lot</vocabulary>. Before the noun it describes, it takes な.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は本をたくさん買いました。

example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は本[ほん]をたくさん買[か]いました。

example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]に猫[ねこ]がたくさんいます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>few</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>a little</vocabulary> word are the same character wearing a kana tail, so they point at the same small amount.
items.reading_mnemonic: After one slash through the small bundle of matchsticks, the cook has only a <reading>skosh</reading> left, 「<reading>すこし</reading>」, just <vocabulary form="少し">a little</vocabulary> to light the stove.

example_sentences.furigana: 水[みず]を少[すこ]し飲[の]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: このコーヒーは少し熱いです。
example_sentences.english: This coffee is a little hot.
example_sentences.furigana: このコーヒーは少[すこ]し熱[あつ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 少し休みます。
example_sentences.furigana: 少[すこ]し休[やす]みます。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's till you ask for a <reading>shot of</reading> milk in your coffee and get <vocabulary>a little</vocabulary> splash, barely enough to cloud it. That thin splash is <reading>ちょっと</reading>.

example_sentences.furigana: ちょっと待[ま]って。

example_sentences.english: This coffee is a bit hot.
example_sentences.furigana: このコーヒーはちょっと熱[あつ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日はちょっと忙しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]はちょっと忙[いそが]しいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You order the set meal with grilled fish. The kitchen has run out, so the waiter brings the same set built around some <vocabulary>other</vocabulary> main.
items.reading_mnemonic: The kitchen ran out of grilled fish, so the waiter calls out like a market <reading>hawker</reading>, 「<reading>ほか</reading>」, and sets down your set meal built around some <vocabulary form="他">other</vocabulary> main.

example_sentences.japanese: 他の色はありますか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Twins show up in the exact same coat. The teacher makes them hang the coats on <vocabulary>separate</vocabulary> hooks so nobody mixes them up.

example_sentences.furigana: これは別[べつ]の本[ほん]です。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 病（びょう）＋気（き）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.

example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は病[びょう]気[き]で仕[し]事[ごと]を休[やす]みました。

items.reading_composition: Irregular — かぜ cannot be assembled from the dictionary readings of 風邪.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>wind</kanji> strong enough to flick a bug off the picnic table turns <kanji>wicked</kanji> and slips down your collar. The chill it leaves behind is a <vocabulary>cold</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the picnic table Grandma Kane sneezes and names the wicked wind that slipped down her collar as the <reading>cause</reading> of her <vocabulary form="風邪">cold</vocabulary>: 「<reading>かぜ</reading>」.
items.description: Identical in sound to the everyday word for wind, and written with that same first character, so only context tells the two apart.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は風邪で学校を休みました。
example_sentences.english: She was absent from school because of a cold.

example_sentences.english: My head hurts because of a cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 風邪[かぜ]で頭[あたま]が痛[いた]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は風邪です。
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は風邪[かぜ]です。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>medicine</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>medicine</vocabulary> word are the same character with the same meaning.

example_sentences.japanese: 朝と晩に薬を飲みます。
example_sentences.english: I take medicine in the morning and at night.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]と晩[ばん]に薬[くすり]を飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は切符をかばんに入れました。
example_sentences.english: I put the ticket in my bag.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は切[きっ]符[ぷ]をかばんに入[い]れました。

example_sentences.japanese: その切符を友達にあげました。

example_sentences.furigana: その切[きっ]符[ぷ]を友[とも]達[だち]にあげました。

example_sentences.furigana: その荷[に]物[もつ]はとても重[おも]いです。

example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]が私[わたし]の荷[に]物[もつ]を運[はこ]んでくれました。
