items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Offer Sei a spoonful of sticky fermented beans and she leans back with a long <reading>ee-eh</reading>, both vowels curling away from you. Stretched out like that, <reading>いいえ</reading> is a gentle <vocabulary>no</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hand someone a small gift and they dip their head and mutter <reading>どうも</reading>. That all-purpose <reading>doh-mo</reading> stands in for <vocabulary>thanks</vocabulary> and a dozen half-sentences nobody bothers to finish.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A delivery guy with a <reading>corn-itchy</reading> sunburn across his neck tips his cap at the door and says <reading>こんにちは</reading>. It is the plain daytime <vocabulary>hello</vocabulary> you switch to once the morning is over.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Say the word slowly and it comes out as <reading>Ohio</reading>, the American state. Land that sound before dawn and you have <reading>おはよう</reading>, the <vocabulary>good morning</vocabulary> you give before anyone has had coffee.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The night baker leaves one leftover <reading>cone bun</reading> on the counter and says <reading>こんばんは</reading> to whoever comes in last. That after-dark greeting is <vocabulary>good evening</vocabulary>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Draw it out on the platform as the train pulls away, the way you would a slow <reading>so long</reading>. That heavy, drawn-out <reading>さようなら</reading> is the <vocabulary>goodbye</vocabulary> that means a good while.
items.description: Heavier than the English 'bye'. It suggests a long separation, so to family or coworkers you will see tomorrow it can sound oddly final; day-to-day partings use lighter phrases.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はさようならと言いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 本当にありがとう。
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]当[とう]にありがとう。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei knocks Grandma Kane's teacup off the mossy step and blurts <reading>ごめんなさい</reading> before it even hits the ground, a rushed <reading>go-men-nah-sigh</reading>. It is the full, please-forgive-me <vocabulary>I'm sorry</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.furigana: 遅[おく]れてごめんなさい。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You shake hands with a man called <reading>Jimmy</reading> who instantly <reading>mashes</reading> your knuckles flat, and out falls <reading>はじめまして</reading>. It is the fixed opening line for a first meeting, <vocabulary>nice to meet you</vocabulary>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At lights-out Sei mumbles <reading>おやすみなさい</reading> into the pillow, a slurred <reading>oh-yah-soo-me-nah-sigh</reading> that trails off into a yawn. It is the <vocabulary>good night</vocabulary> you say heading to sleep, not the one you say leaving a room.

example_sentences.japanese: 母におやすみなさいと言いました。

example_sentences.furigana: 子[こ]供[ども]たちはおやすみなさいと言[い]って、寝[ね]ました。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Lift your chopsticks over a steaming bowl and say <reading>いただきます</reading>, close enough to <reading>eat-a-duck-ee</reading> to stick. It is the set phrase you say before eating, <vocabulary>let's eat</vocabulary>, with a nod of thanks for the food.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Too stuffed to move after dinner, you flop onto the <reading>Gucci sofa, Ma</reading> and let out a long groan. That groan, 「<reading>ごちそうさま</reading>」, is exactly how you say <vocabulary>thanks for the meal</vocabulary> once your plate is clean.

example_sentences.japanese: 友達の家でご飯を食べて、ごちそうさまと言いました。

example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]の家[いえ]でご飯[はん]を食[た]べて、ごちそうさまと言[い]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You pause at the <kanji>go</kanji> crossroads and call back to the house before you step out. That call is <vocabulary>I'm off (going and coming back)</vocabulary>, and the crossroads is your promise to walk back through it by evening.

example_sentences.japanese: ちょっとコンビニに行ってきます。
example_sentences.english: I'm just going to the convenience store.
example_sentences.furigana: ちょっとコンビニに行[い]ってきます。

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行に行ってきます。
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]に行[い]ってきます。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You fling open the front door with a magician's <reading>ta-da, I'm a</reading> wizard flourish. That same sound, 「<reading>ただいま</reading>」, is exactly how you call out <vocabulary>I'm home</vocabulary> the moment you step inside.

example_sentences.japanese: ただいま。今日は忙しかったです。
example_sentences.furigana: ただいま。今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しかったです。

example_sentences.japanese: ただいま、お父さん。
example_sentences.furigana: ただいま、お父[とう]さん。

example_sentences.japanese: ただいま。家族はまだ晩ご飯を食べていません。
example_sentences.english: I'm home. My family hasn't eaten dinner yet.
example_sentences.furigana: ただいま。家[か]族[ぞく]はまだ晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べていません。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — お＋帰（かえ）＋りなさい.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You hand the sweeper to whoever just <kanji>returned</kanji> through the front door, and the greeting that goes with it is <vocabulary>welcome back</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 帰 is 「かえ」 from 帰る, so <vocabulary>welcome back</vocabulary> is <reading>おかえりなさい</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: お父さん、お帰りなさい。
example_sentences.furigana: お父[とう]さん、お帰[かえ]りなさい。

example_sentences.japanese: お帰りなさい。晩ご飯を作りました。
example_sentences.furigana: お帰[かえ]りなさい。晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を作[つく]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はうちに帰って、お帰りなさいと言いました。
example_sentences.english: She came home, and I said welcome back to her.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はうちに帰[かえ]って、お帰[かえ]りなさいと言[い]いました。
